The Great Molasses Flood destruction caused by a storage tank bursting and a 26 feet tall molasses wave rushed through the streets at 35 mph, killing 21 and injuring 150. Boston. 1919

The Great Boston Molasses Flood occurred on January 15, 1919, in the North End neighborhood of Boston, Massachusetts. After a large molasses storage tank collapsed, a molasses wave up to 26 feet high rushed through the streets at an estimated 35 miles per hour (56 kilometers per hour), killing 21 and injuring 150.

The disaster occurred at the Purity Distilling Company located in Boston's North End. The tank was 50 feet (15 meters) tall, 90 feet (27 meters) in diameter, and contained as much as 2,300,000 U.S. gallons (8,700 cubic meters). The molasses wave was of sufficient force to damage the girders of the adjacent elevated railway, as may be seen here. Several blocks were flooded to a depth of 2 to 3 feet (60 to 90 centimeters).

The cleanup in the immediate area took "weeks", with more than 300 people contributing to the effort. The cleanup in the rest of Greater Boston and its suburbs would take an indefinably longer time. Rescue workers, cleanup crews and sight-seers had tracked molasses through the streets and spread it to subway platforms, to the seats inside trains and streetcars, to pay telephone handsets, into homes and to countless other places. "Everything a Bostonian touched was sticky."
